title: Space Potatoes nickname comes from Betty and Barney Hill 1961 New Hampshire UFO encounter

content:
How a UFO encounter in 1961 led to Double-A New Hampshire’s weirdest alternate identity

This browser does not support the video element.

MANCHESTER, N.H. -- Taylor Fisher had already been working in Minor League Baseball for about 10 years when he was hired by the New Hampshire Fisher Cats (Double-A affiliate of the Toronto Blue Jays), yet he immediately saw that he was entering a whole new world.

“I walked in on my first day as general manager here, and on the white board next to me it just said, ‘Space Potatoes,’” Fisher recalled. “I said, ‘What the heck did that mean?’”

That was in 2024. Now, at the end of 2026, Fisher and baseball fans across New England know exactly what the phrase means. The New Hampshire Space Potatoes have become a beloved alternate identity, adopted by the Fisher Cats for a total of nine home games over the past two seasons.

But where did "Space Potatoes" come from? It’s an idea that ties together two little-known pieces of New Hampshire history.

The first pertains to historical fact. In 1719, on land in the current-day New Hampshire town of Derry, Scots-Irish settlers planted the first white potatoes grown in North America. In 2013, fourth graders from the Derry Village School successfully lobbied to have the white potato named the official state vegetable.

The second sits at the nexus of the known universe and the realm of possibility. About 80 miles north-northwest of the Fisher Cats’ ballpark in Manchester is the spot where the first widely reported alien abduction in American history allegedly took place in 1961.

“So, you mash those two together, you get the Space Potatoes,” Fisher Cats assistant GM Andrew Marais said.

Marais, like many Space Potatoes fans, is a UFO believer. Every year when he takes an hour drive into the White Mountains, he stops at an alien-themed gas station and passes a roadside marker on the highway in the town of Lincoln. That sign reads:

On the night of September 19-20, 1961, Portsmouth, NH couple Betty and Barney Hill experienced a close encounter with an unidentified flying object and two hours of “lost” time while driving south on Rte. 3 near Lincoln. They filed an official Air Force Project Blue Book report of a brightly-lit cigar-shaped craft the next day, but were not public with their story until it was leaked to the Boston Traveler in 1965. This was the first widely-reported UFO abduction in the United States.

That’s the story. Is there anything to it?

Michael Clair, MLB.com’s resident expert on international baseball and intergalactic lifeforms, says it’s worth considering the Hills’ accounts of the incident as well as the way those accounts become public. Emphasizing that the Hills were an interracial couple and were both civil workers who never sought or wanted media attention, Clair points out that many of the details of their abduction weren't revealed until after they underwent hypnotic regression therapy years after the incident.

Among those details: the Hills pulled off the highway onto a small, rural road and encountered beings who encouraged the couple to get out of their car. They were brought onto a craft, separated, examined and questioned.

“At one point they come into Betty’s room,” Clair said, “and start pulling on her teeth and saying, ‘Why aren’t your teeth coming out? Why are Barney’s teeth coming out?’ (They didn’t say his name.) And she said, ‘He has dentures. It happens when you get older.’ They didn’t understand age. They asked her multiple times, ‘What is older?’ She had to explain human aging to them.

“They also both remember grey-faced creatures with a larger skull ... [a] forehead that gets narrower below with almost no nose and a flat mouth. That is the common depiction of what is commonly known as ‘greys,’ grey aliens.”

Austin Cates, the Blue Jays’ No. 30 prospect, didn’t learn the specifics of the Hill incident until a couple months after he’d already pitched as a Space Potato. A native of Nevada, Cates has long been open to the possibility that Area 51 holds proof of extraterrestrial life. Hearing that the Hills initially reported their experience only to the government, he was convinced they’d told the truth.

“That’s crazy!” he said. “Yeah. Aliens are real. I’ll throw it out there. I’ll say they’re real.”

Waiting in line at the gates to receive a Trey Yesevage-Space Potatoes bobblehead before the game on Sept. 18, a regular at Fisher Cats games named Jake was also pretty sure the story was legitimate.

“If somebody says it happened, more than likely there’s some truth to it,” he said.

And if word of the Fisher Cats’ alternate identity should travel? If flying saucers were to show up at Delta Dental Stadium?

It’s a risk the New Hampshire front office is willing to take.

“It would boost attendance,” Fisher said, “and that’s what matters. Butts in seats.”
